elements. We hit this with the argsort of 4420 candidates in the non-max
suppression of a detection model, where the sort dispatch alone took
about 18 ms on x86-64, many times the rest of the model.

A faster in-place algorithm is not stable, and stability turned out to
matter: the bubble sort keeps equal elements in input order when the
comparator is non-strict (`oge`, `sle`, ...), because it then never
swaps them. The Torch frontend emits exactly such comparators, and e.g.
`onnx.NonMaxSuppression` expects the lowest index first among boxes with
the same score (`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes` failed with a
plain heapsort). With a strict comparator (`ogt`, `slt`, ...) the bubble
sort is not stable: keys `1, 1, 2, 2, 0` sorted descending together with
their indices return the indices `3 2 1 0 4`.

So this PR makes stability explicit and picks the algorithm from it.

## This PR

### `is_stable`

The op gets an `is_stable` attribute, false by default and only printed
when set:

```mlir
%0:2 = iree_linalg_ext.sort dimension(0) is_stable(true)
    ins(%keys, %payload : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>)
    outs(%init0, %init1 : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>) {
  ^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_payload: i32, %rhs_payload: i32):
    %before = arith.cmpf ogt, %lhs, %rhs : f32
    iree_linalg_ext.yield %before : i1
} -> tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>
```

The op description now defines the terms. The comparator *does not
order* two elements if it returns the same value for both argument
orders (both `false` with a strict comparison, both `true` with a
non-strict one). Without `is_stable` such elements end up in unspecified
order. With `is_stable` they keep their input order: an element only
moves in front of another one if the comparator returns `true` for that
order and `false` for the opposite one. This definition is the same for
strict and non-strict comparators.

### Lowering variants

All variants are in place: they need no storage besides the operands, so
nothing changes for bufferization or stack usage, and they work for
dynamic sizes and on every backend. The loop nest built from the
iteration domain is unchanged; a slice is sorted in the first iteration
of the loop over the sort dimension, where the inputs were already
copied to the outputs. Operands that are sorted in place are no longer
copied onto themselves.

**1. Not stable: heapsort.** O(n log n) comparisons.

```
for (root = n/2 - 1; root >= 0; --root)      // build the heap
  siftDown(root, slice[root], n)
for (end = n - 1; end > 0; --end) {          // move its first element
  last = slice[end]; slice[end] = slice[0]   // behind the shrinking heap
  siftDown(0, last, end)
}
```

`siftDown` is a `scf.while` that moves an element down until neither
child has to be placed after it.

**2. Stable: binary insertion sort.** O(n log n) comparisons, but O(n^2)
element moves. It is the fallback that always works: a stable sort with
O(n log n) moves needs scratch storage of the operand size (merge sort),
which a dispatch can only take from the stack and which is unbounded for
dynamic sizes.

```
for (i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
  element = slice[i]
  lo = <first position in the sorted prefix [0, i) whose element has to stay
        behind `element`, by binary search>
  for (j = i; j > lo; --j) slice[j] = slice[j - 1]
  slice[lo] = element
}
```

The search uses "strictly before" (comparator true for this order and
false for the opposite one), so that elements the comparator does not
order are never reordered.

**3. Stable with a position operand: heapsort with a tie-break
(canonicalization).** If an operand of a stable sort holds the positions
along the sort dimension (a `linalg.generic` yielding `linalg.index`,
which is what `aten.sort` passes as indices), it tells the input order
of any two elements. `FoldSortStabilityIntoComparator` extends the
comparator to order the elements it does not order itself by position,
and clears `is_stable`:

```mlir
^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_pos: i64, %rhs_pos: i64):
  %before = arith.cmpf oge, %lhs, %rhs : f32
  %after = arith.cmpf oge, %rhs, %lhs : f32
  %ordered = arith.xori %before, %after : i1
  %lower_pos = arith.cmpi slt, %lhs_pos, %rhs_pos : i64
  %result = arith.select %ordered, %before, %lower_pos : i1
  iree_linalg_ext.yield %result : i1
```

The comparator is then a strict total order: no two elements are left
without a defined order, so every sorting algorithm returns the result
of the stable sort and the op can use variant 1. The cost is a second
evaluation of the comparator per comparison.

The rewrite only applies if the sorted positions are used. If they are
not, `RemoveUnusedSortOpResults` drops the operand as before, instead of
keeping its buffer in the dispatch just for the comparator; the sort
then stays stable (variant 2, or variant 4).

**4. Stable but unobservable: heapsort (canonicalization).**

operand whose comparator is an integer comparison of its two arguments.
Elements that such a comparator does not order are the same value, so
their order cannot be observed. Floats are left alone (`0.0` and `-0.0`
compare equal but differ).

dropped before, and since StableHLO comparators are usually strict,

[LinalgExt] Add is_stable to sort and replace the bubble sort lowering (#25262)

## Context

`iree_linalg_ext.sort` lowers to a bubble sort:
`SortOp::generateScalarImplementation` emits one sweep of n-1
compare-swaps for each of the n iterations of the loop over the sort
dimension, with no early exit. Sorting n elements takes O(n^2) steps,
which shows up as soon as the sorted dimension has a few thousand
elements. We hit this with the argsort of 4420 candidates in the non-max
suppression of a detection model, where the sort dispatch alone took
about 18 ms on x86-64, many times the rest of the model.

A faster in-place algorithm is not stable, and stability turned out to
matter: the bubble sort keeps equal elements in input order when the
comparator is non-strict (`oge`, `sle`, ...), because it then never
swaps them. The Torch frontend emits exactly such comparators, and e.g.
`onnx.NonMaxSuppression` expects the lowest index first among boxes with
the same score (`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes` failed with a
plain heapsort). With a strict comparator (`ogt`, `slt`, ...) the bubble
sort is not stable: keys `1, 1, 2, 2, 0` sorted descending together with
their indices return the indices `3 2 1 0 4`.

So this PR makes stability explicit and picks the algorithm from it.

## This PR

### `is_stable`

The op gets an `is_stable` attribute, false by default and only printed
when set:

```mlir
%0:2 = iree_linalg_ext.sort dimension(0) is_stable(true)
    ins(%keys, %payload : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>)
    outs(%init0, %init1 : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>) {
  ^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_payload: i32, %rhs_payload: i32):
    %before = arith.cmpf ogt, %lhs, %rhs : f32
    iree_linalg_ext.yield %before : i1
} -> tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>
```

The op description now defines the terms. The comparator *does not
order* two elements if it returns the same value for both argument
orders (both `false` with a strict comparison, both `true` with a
non-strict one). Without `is_stable` such elements end up in unspecified
order. With `is_stable` they keep their input order: an element only
moves in front of another one if the comparator returns `true` for that
order and `false` for the opposite one. This definition is the same for
strict and non-strict comparators.

### Lowering variants

All variants are in place: they need no storage besides the operands, so
nothing changes for bufferization or stack usage, and they work for
dynamic sizes and on every backend. The loop nest built from the
iteration domain is unchanged; a slice is sorted in the first iteration
of the loop over the sort dimension, where the inputs were already
copied to the outputs. Operands that are sorted in place are no longer
copied onto themselves.

**1. Not stable: heapsort.** O(n log n) comparisons.

```
for (root = n/2 - 1; root >= 0; --root)      // build the heap
  siftDown(root, slice[root], n)
for (end = n - 1; end > 0; --end) {          // move its first element
  last = slice[end]; slice[end] = slice[0]   // behind the shrinking heap
  siftDown(0, last, end)
}
```

`siftDown` is a `scf.while` that moves an element down until neither
child has to be placed after it.

**2. Stable: binary insertion sort.** O(n log n) comparisons, but O(n^2)
element moves. It is the fallback that always works: a stable sort with
O(n log n) moves needs scratch storage of the operand size (merge sort),
which a dispatch can only take from the stack and which is unbounded for
dynamic sizes.

```
for (i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
  element = slice[i]
  lo = <first position in the sorted prefix [0, i) whose element has to stay
        behind `element`, by binary search>
  for (j = i; j > lo; --j) slice[j] = slice[j - 1]
  slice[lo] = element
}
```

The search uses "strictly before" (comparator true for this order and
false for the opposite one), so that elements the comparator does not
order are never reordered.

**3. Stable with a position operand: heapsort with a tie-break
(canonicalization).** If an operand of a stable sort holds the positions
along the sort dimension (a `linalg.generic` yielding `linalg.index`,
which is what `aten.sort` passes as indices), it tells the input order
of any two elements. `FoldSortStabilityIntoComparator` extends the
comparator to order the elements it does not order itself by position,
and clears `is_stable`:

```mlir
^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_pos: i64, %rhs_pos: i64):
  %before = arith.cmpf oge, %lhs, %rhs : f32
  %after = arith.cmpf oge, %rhs, %lhs : f32
  %ordered = arith.xori %before, %after : i1
  %lower_pos = arith.cmpi slt, %lhs_pos, %rhs_pos : i64
  %result = arith.select %ordered, %before, %lower_pos : i1
  iree_linalg_ext.yield %result : i1
```

The comparator is then a strict total order: no two elements are left
without a defined order, so every sorting algorithm returns the result
of the stable sort and the op can use variant 1. The cost is a second
evaluation of the comparator per comparison.

The rewrite only applies if the sorted positions are used. If they are
not, `RemoveUnusedSortOpResults` drops the operand as before, instead of
keeping its buffer in the dispatch just for the comparator; the sort
then stays stable (variant 2, or variant 4).

**4. Stable but unobservable: heapsort (canonicalization).**
`DropUnobservableSortStability` clears `is_stable` for a single integer
operand whose comparator is an integer comparison of its two arguments.
Elements that such a comparator does not order are the same value, so
their order cannot be observed. Floats are left alone (`0.0` and `-0.0`
compare equal but differ).

### Frontends

* **Torch:** the conversion of `tm_tensor.sort` always sets `is_stable`,
since those sorts have relied on the stable behaviour. With the index
operand of `aten.sort` they get variant 3; a sort that only uses the
values gets variant 2 (floats) or 4 (integers).
* **StableHLO:** `is_stable` of `stablehlo.sort` is passed on. It was
dropped before, and since StableHLO comparators are usually strict,
stable StableHLO sorts were in fact not stable.

### Things to know

* **Unstable sorts order ties differently than before.** That is only
allowed for sorts without `is_stable`, i.e. StableHLO sorts with
`is_stable = false` and ops built directly.
* **NaN.** An ordered float comparison does not order NaN with any
value, which makes the comparator inconsistent (it orders `1.0` and
`2.0`, but neither with NaN). The op description now requires a
consistent comparator. In a simulation of the old lowering on a few

[LinalgExt] Add is_stable to sort and replace the bubble sort lowering (#25262)

## Context

`iree_linalg_ext.sort` lowers to a bubble sort:
`SortOp::generateScalarImplementation` emits one sweep of n-1
compare-swaps for each of the n iterations of the loop over the sort
dimension, with no early exit. Sorting n elements takes O(n^2) steps,
which shows up as soon as the sorted dimension has a few thousand
elements. We hit this with the argsort of 4420 candidates in the non-max
suppression of a detection model, where the sort dispatch alone took
about 18 ms on x86-64, many times the rest of the model.

A faster in-place algorithm is not stable, and stability turned out to
matter: the bubble sort keeps equal elements in input order when the
comparator is non-strict (`oge`, `sle`, ...), because it then never
swaps them. The Torch frontend emits exactly such comparators, and e.g.
`onnx.NonMaxSuppression` expects the lowest index first among boxes with
the same score (`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes` failed with a
plain heapsort). With a strict comparator (`ogt`, `slt`, ...) the bubble
sort is not stable: keys `1, 1, 2, 2, 0` sorted descending together with
their indices return the indices `3 2 1 0 4`.

So this PR makes stability explicit and picks the algorithm from it.

## This PR

### `is_stable`

The op gets an `is_stable` attribute, false by default and only printed
when set:

```mlir
%0:2 = iree_linalg_ext.sort dimension(0) is_stable(true)
    ins(%keys, %payload : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>)
    outs(%init0, %init1 : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>) {
  ^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_payload: i32, %rhs_payload: i32):
    %before = arith.cmpf ogt, %lhs, %rhs : f32
    iree_linalg_ext.yield %before : i1
} -> tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>
```

The op description now defines the terms. The comparator *does not
order* two elements if it returns the same value for both argument
orders (both `false` with a strict comparison, both `true` with a
non-strict one). Without `is_stable` such elements end up in unspecified
order. With `is_stable` they keep their input order: an element only
moves in front of another one if the comparator returns `true` for that
order and `false` for the opposite one. This definition is the same for
strict and non-strict comparators.

### Lowering variants

All variants are in place: they need no storage besides the operands, so
nothing changes for bufferization or stack usage, and they work for
dynamic sizes and on every backend. The loop nest built from the
iteration domain is unchanged; a slice is sorted in the first iteration
of the loop over the sort dimension, where the inputs were already
copied to the outputs. Operands that are sorted in place are no longer
copied onto themselves.

**1. Not stable: heapsort.** O(n log n) comparisons.

```
for (root = n/2 - 1; root >= 0; --root)      // build the heap
  siftDown(root, slice[root], n)
for (end = n - 1; end > 0; --end) {          // move its first element
  last = slice[end]; slice[end] = slice[0]   // behind the shrinking heap
  siftDown(0, last, end)
}
```

`siftDown` is a `scf.while` that moves an element down until neither
child has to be placed after it.

**2. Stable: binary insertion sort.** O(n log n) comparisons, but O(n^2)
element moves. It is the fallback that always works: a stable sort with
O(n log n) moves needs scratch storage of the operand size (merge sort),
which a dispatch can only take from the stack and which is unbounded for
dynamic sizes.

```
for (i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
  element = slice[i]
  lo = <first position in the sorted prefix [0, i) whose element has to stay
        behind `element`, by binary search>
  for (j = i; j > lo; --j) slice[j] = slice[j - 1]
  slice[lo] = element
}
```

The search uses "strictly before" (comparator true for this order and
false for the opposite one), so that elements the comparator does not
order are never reordered.

**3. Stable with a position operand: heapsort with a tie-break
(canonicalization).** If an operand of a stable sort holds the positions
along the sort dimension (a `linalg.generic` yielding `linalg.index`,
which is what `aten.sort` passes as indices), it tells the input order
of any two elements. `FoldSortStabilityIntoComparator` extends the
comparator to order the elements it does not order itself by position,
and clears `is_stable`:

```mlir
^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_pos: i64, %rhs_pos: i64):
  %before = arith.cmpf oge, %lhs, %rhs : f32
  %after = arith.cmpf oge, %rhs, %lhs : f32
  %ordered = arith.xori %before, %after : i1
  %lower_pos = arith.cmpi slt, %lhs_pos, %rhs_pos : i64
  %result = arith.select %ordered, %before, %lower_pos : i1
  iree_linalg_ext.yield %result : i1
```

The comparator is then a strict total order: no two elements are left
without a defined order, so every sorting algorithm returns the result
of the stable sort and the op can use variant 1. The cost is a second
evaluation of the comparator per comparison.

The rewrite only applies if the sorted positions are used. If they are
not, `RemoveUnusedSortOpResults` drops the operand as before, instead of
keeping its buffer in the dispatch just for the comparator; the sort
then stays stable (variant 2, or variant 4).

**4. Stable but unobservable: heapsort (canonicalization).**
`DropUnobservableSortStability` clears `is_stable` for a single integer
operand whose comparator is an integer comparison of its two arguments.
Elements that such a comparator does not order are the same value, so
their order cannot be observed. Floats are left alone (`0.0` and `-0.0`
compare equal but differ).

### Frontends

* **Torch:** the conversion of `tm_tensor.sort` always sets `is_stable`,
since those sorts have relied on the stable behaviour. With the index
operand of `aten.sort` they get variant 3; a sort that only uses the
values gets variant 2 (floats) or 4 (integers).
* **StableHLO:** `is_stable` of `stablehlo.sort` is passed on. It was
dropped before, and since StableHLO comparators are usually strict,
stable StableHLO sorts were in fact not stable.

### Things to know

* **Unstable sorts order ties differently than before.** That is only
allowed for sorts without `is_stable`, i.e. StableHLO sorts with
`is_stable = false` and ops built directly.
* **NaN.** An ordered float comparison does not order NaN with any
value, which makes the comparator inconsistent (it orders `1.0` and
`2.0`, but neither with NaN). The op description now requires a
consistent comparator. In a simulation of the old lowering on a few
inputs, NaNs stayed at their input positions and the other values were
sorted around them. With the new lowerings the other values can come out

keys needs a comparator that orders them (e.g. NaN last, as `torch.sort`
does); the Torch comparators do not do that today.
* `topk_v2` keeps its bubble sort over the k outputs; it is not touched
here.

`iree_linalg_ext.sort` lowers to a bubble sort:

compare-swaps for each of the n iterations of the loop over the sort
dimension, with no early exit. Sorting n elements takes O(n^2) steps,
which shows up as soon as the sorted dimension has a few thousand
elements. We hit this with the argsort of 4420 candidates in the non-max
suppression of a detection model, where the sort dispatch alone took
about 18 ms on x86-64, many times the rest of the model.

A faster in-place algorithm is not stable, and stability turned out to
matter: the bubble sort keeps equal elements in input order when the
comparator is non-strict (`oge`, `sle`, ...), because it then never
swaps them. The Torch frontend emits exactly such comparators, and e.g.
`onnx.NonMaxSuppression` expects the lowest index first among boxes with
the same score (`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes` failed with a
plain heapsort). With a strict comparator (`ogt`, `slt`, ...) the bubble
sort is not stable: keys `1, 1, 2, 2, 0` sorted descending together with
their indices return the indices `3 2 1 0 4`.

So this PR makes stability explicit and picks the algorithm from it.

## This PR

### `is_stable`

The op gets an `is_stable` attribute, false by default and only printed
when set:

```mlir
%0:2 = iree_linalg_ext.sort dimension(0) is_stable(true)
    ins(%keys, %payload : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>)
    outs(%init0, %init1 : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>) {
  ^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_payload: i32, %rhs_payload: i32):
    %before = arith.cmpf ogt, %lhs, %rhs : f32
    iree_linalg_ext.yield %before : i1
} -> tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>
```

The op description now defines the terms. The comparator *does not
order* two elements if it returns the same value for both argument
orders (both `false` with a strict comparison, both `true` with a
non-strict one). Without `is_stable` such elements end up in unspecified
order. With `is_stable` they keep their input order: an element only
moves in front of another one if the comparator returns `true` for that
order and `false` for the opposite one. This definition is the same for
strict and non-strict comparators.

### Lowering variants

All variants are in place: they need no storage besides the operands, so
nothing changes for bufferization or stack usage, and they work for
dynamic sizes and on every backend. The loop nest built from the
iteration domain is unchanged; a slice is sorted in the first iteration
of the loop over the sort dimension, where the inputs were already
copied to the outputs. Operands that are sorted in place are no longer
copied onto themselves.

**1. Not stable: heapsort.** O(n log n) comparisons.

```
for (root = n/2 - 1; root >= 0; --root)      // build the heap
  siftDown(root, slice[root], n)
for (end = n - 1; end > 0; --end) {          // move its first element
  last = slice[end]; slice[end] = slice[0]   // behind the shrinking heap
  siftDown(0, last, end)
}
```

`siftDown` is a `scf.while` that moves an element down until neither
child has to be placed after it.

**2. Stable: binary insertion sort.** O(n log n) comparisons, but O(n^2)
element moves. It is the fallback that always works: a stable sort with
O(n log n) moves needs scratch storage of the operand size (merge sort),
which a dispatch can only take from the stack and which is unbounded for
dynamic sizes.

```
for (i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
  element = slice[i]
  lo = <first position in the sorted prefix [0, i) whose element has to stay
        behind `element`, by binary search>
  for (j = i; j > lo; --j) slice[j] = slice[j - 1]
  slice[lo] = element
}
```

The search uses "strictly before" (comparator true for this order and
false for the opposite one), so that elements the comparator does not
order are never reordered.

**3. Stable with a position operand: heapsort with a tie-break
(canonicalization).** If an operand of a stable sort holds the positions
along the sort dimension (a `linalg.generic` yielding `linalg.index`,
which is what `aten.sort` passes as indices), it tells the input order
of any two elements. `FoldSortStabilityIntoComparator` extends the
comparator to order the elements it does not order itself by position,
and clears `is_stable`:

```mlir
^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_pos: i64, %rhs_pos: i64):
  %before = arith.cmpf oge, %lhs, %rhs : f32
  %after = arith.cmpf oge, %rhs, %lhs : f32
  %ordered = arith.xori %before, %after : i1
  %lower_pos = arith.cmpi slt, %lhs_pos, %rhs_pos : i64
  %result = arith.select %ordered, %before, %lower_pos : i1
  iree_linalg_ext.yield %result : i1
```

The comparator is then a strict total order: no two elements are left
without a defined order, so every sorting algorithm returns the result
of the stable sort and the op can use variant 1. The cost is a second
evaluation of the comparator per comparison.

The rewrite only applies if the sorted positions are used. If they are
not, `RemoveUnusedSortOpResults` drops the operand as before, instead of
keeping its buffer in the dispatch just for the comparator; the sort
then stays stable (variant 2, or variant 4).

**4. Stable but unobservable: heapsort (canonicalization).**
`DropUnobservableSortStability` clears `is_stable` for a single integer
operand whose comparator is an integer comparison of its two arguments.
Elements that such a comparator does not order are the same value, so
their order cannot be observed. Floats are left alone (`0.0` and `-0.0`
compare equal but differ).

dropped before, and since StableHLO comparators are usually strict,

* **Unstable sorts order ties differently than before.** That is only

[LinalgExt] Add is_stable to sort and replace the bubble sort lowering (#25262)

## Context

`iree_linalg_ext.sort` lowers to a bubble sort:
`SortOp::generateScalarImplementation` emits one sweep of n-1
compare-swaps for each of the n iterations of the loop over the sort
dimension, with no early exit. Sorting n elements takes O(n^2) steps,
which shows up as soon as the sorted dimension has a few thousand
elements. We hit this with the argsort of 4420 candidates in the non-max
suppression of a detection model, where the sort dispatch alone took
about 18 ms on x86-64, many times the rest of the model.

A faster in-place algorithm is not stable, and stability turned out to
matter: the bubble sort keeps equal elements in input order when the
comparator is non-strict (`oge`, `sle`, ...), because it then never
swaps them. The Torch frontend emits exactly such comparators, and e.g.
`onnx.NonMaxSuppression` expects the lowest index first among boxes with
the same score (`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes` failed with a
plain heapsort). With a strict comparator (`ogt`, `slt`, ...) the bubble
sort is not stable: keys `1, 1, 2, 2, 0` sorted descending together with
their indices return the indices `3 2 1 0 4`.

So this PR makes stability explicit and picks the algorithm from it.

## This PR

### `is_stable`

The op gets an `is_stable` attribute, false by default and only printed
when set:

```mlir
%0:2 = iree_linalg_ext.sort dimension(0) is_stable(true)
    ins(%keys, %payload : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>)
    outs(%init0, %init1 : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>) {
  ^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_payload: i32, %rhs_payload: i32):
    %before = arith.cmpf ogt, %lhs, %rhs : f32
    iree_linalg_ext.yield %before : i1
} -> tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>
```

The op description now defines the terms. The comparator *does not
order* two elements if it returns the same value for both argument
orders (both `false` with a strict comparison, both `true` with a
non-strict one). Without `is_stable` such elements end up in unspecified
order. With `is_stable` they keep their input order: an element only
moves in front of another one if the comparator returns `true` for that
order and `false` for the opposite one. This definition is the same for
strict and non-strict comparators.

### Lowering variants

All variants are in place: they need no storage besides the operands, so
nothing changes for bufferization or stack usage, and they work for
dynamic sizes and on every backend. The loop nest built from the
iteration domain is unchanged; a slice is sorted in the first iteration
of the loop over the sort dimension, where the inputs were already
copied to the outputs. Operands that are sorted in place are no longer
copied onto themselves.

**1. Not stable: heapsort.** O(n log n) comparisons.

```
for (root = n/2 - 1; root >= 0; --root)      // build the heap
  siftDown(root, slice[root], n)
for (end = n - 1; end > 0; --end) {          // move its first element
  last = slice[end]; slice[end] = slice[0]   // behind the shrinking heap
  siftDown(0, last, end)
}
```

`siftDown` is a `scf.while` that moves an element down until neither
child has to be placed after it.

**2. Stable: binary insertion sort.** O(n log n) comparisons, but O(n^2)
element moves. It is the fallback that always works: a stable sort with
O(n log n) moves needs scratch storage of the operand size (merge sort),
which a dispatch can only take from the stack and which is unbounded for
dynamic sizes.

```
for (i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
  element = slice[i]
  lo = <first position in the sorted prefix [0, i) whose element has to stay
        behind `element`, by binary search>
  for (j = i; j > lo; --j) slice[j] = slice[j - 1]
  slice[lo] = element
}
```

The search uses "strictly before" (comparator true for this order and
false for the opposite one), so that elements the comparator does not
order are never reordered.

**3. Stable with a position operand: heapsort with a tie-break
(canonicalization).** If an operand of a stable sort holds the positions
along the sort dimension (a `linalg.generic` yielding `linalg.index`,
which is what `aten.sort` passes as indices), it tells the input order
of any two elements. `FoldSortStabilityIntoComparator` extends the
comparator to order the elements it does not order itself by position,
and clears `is_stable`:

```mlir
^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_pos: i64, %rhs_pos: i64):
  %before = arith.cmpf oge, %lhs, %rhs : f32
  %after = arith.cmpf oge, %rhs, %lhs : f32
  %ordered = arith.xori %before, %after : i1
  %lower_pos = arith.cmpi slt, %lhs_pos, %rhs_pos : i64
  %result = arith.select %ordered, %before, %lower_pos : i1
  iree_linalg_ext.yield %result : i1
```

The comparator is then a strict total order: no two elements are left
without a defined order, so every sorting algorithm returns the result
of the stable sort and the op can use variant 1. The cost is a second
evaluation of the comparator per comparison.

The rewrite only applies if the sorted positions are used. If they are
not, `RemoveUnusedSortOpResults` drops the operand as before, instead of
keeping its buffer in the dispatch just for the comparator; the sort
then stays stable (variant 2, or variant 4).

**4. Stable but unobservable: heapsort (canonicalization).**
`DropUnobservableSortStability` clears `is_stable` for a single integer
operand whose comparator is an integer comparison of its two arguments.
Elements that such a comparator does not order are the same value, so
their order cannot be observed. Floats are left alone (`0.0` and `-0.0`
compare equal but differ).

### Frontends

* **Torch:** the conversion of `tm_tensor.sort` always sets `is_stable`,
since those sorts have relied on the stable behaviour. With the index
operand of `aten.sort` they get variant 3; a sort that only uses the
values gets variant 2 (floats) or 4 (integers).
* **StableHLO:** `is_stable` of `stablehlo.sort` is passed on. It was
dropped before, and since StableHLO comparators are usually strict,
stable StableHLO sorts were in fact not stable.

### Things to know

* **Unstable sorts order ties differently than before.** That is only
allowed for sorts without `is_stable`, i.e. StableHLO sorts with
`is_stable = false` and ops built directly.
* **NaN.** An ordered float comparison does not order NaN with any
value, which makes the comparator inconsistent (it orders `1.0` and
`2.0`, but neither with NaN). The op description now requires a
consistent comparator. In a simulation of the old lowering on a few
inputs, NaNs stayed at their input positions and the other values were
sorted around them. With the new lowerings the other values can come out
unsorted as well, e.g. `3, NaN, 1, 2, NaN, 5, 4, 0` sorted with `ogt`

keys needs a comparator that orders them (e.g. NaN last, as `torch.sort`
does); the Torch comparators do not do that today.

here.

0.127 ms | 158x |

ms | 5.9x |

plain heapsort). With a strict comparator (`ogt`, `slt`, ...) the bubble
sort is not stable: keys `1, 1, 2, 2, 0` sorted descending together with

[LinalgExt] Add is_stable to sort and replace the bubble sort lowering (#25262)

## Context

`iree_linalg_ext.sort` lowers to a bubble sort:
`SortOp::generateScalarImplementation` emits one sweep of n-1
compare-swaps for each of the n iterations of the loop over the sort
dimension, with no early exit. Sorting n elements takes O(n^2) steps,
which shows up as soon as the sorted dimension has a few thousand
elements. We hit this with the argsort of 4420 candidates in the non-max
suppression of a detection model, where the sort dispatch alone took
about 18 ms on x86-64, many times the rest of the model.

A faster in-place algorithm is not stable, and stability turned out to
matter: the bubble sort keeps equal elements in input order when the
comparator is non-strict (`oge`, `sle`, ...), because it then never
swaps them. The Torch frontend emits exactly such comparators, and e.g.
`onnx.NonMaxSuppression` expects the lowest index first among boxes with
the same score (`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes` failed with a
plain heapsort). With a strict comparator (`ogt`, `slt`, ...) the bubble
sort is not stable: keys `1, 1, 2, 2, 0` sorted descending together with
their indices return the indices `3 2 1 0 4`.

So this PR makes stability explicit and picks the algorithm from it.

## This PR

### `is_stable`

The op gets an `is_stable` attribute, false by default and only printed
when set:

```mlir
%0:2 = iree_linalg_ext.sort dimension(0) is_stable(true)
    ins(%keys, %payload : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>)
    outs(%init0, %init1 : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>) {
  ^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_payload: i32, %rhs_payload: i32):
    %before = arith.cmpf ogt, %lhs, %rhs : f32
    iree_linalg_ext.yield %before : i1
} -> tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>
```

The op description now defines the terms. The comparator *does not
order* two elements if it returns the same value for both argument
orders (both `false` with a strict comparison, both `true` with a
non-strict one). Without `is_stable` such elements end up in unspecified
order. With `is_stable` they keep their input order: an element only
moves in front of another one if the comparator returns `true` for that
order and `false` for the opposite one. This definition is the same for
strict and non-strict comparators.

### Lowering variants

All variants are in place: they need no storage besides the operands, so
nothing changes for bufferization or stack usage, and they work for
dynamic sizes and on every backend. The loop nest built from the
iteration domain is unchanged; a slice is sorted in the first iteration
of the loop over the sort dimension, where the inputs were already
copied to the outputs. Operands that are sorted in place are no longer
copied onto themselves.

**1. Not stable: heapsort.** O(n log n) comparisons.

```
for (root = n/2 - 1; root >= 0; --root)      // build the heap
  siftDown(root, slice[root], n)
for (end = n - 1; end > 0; --end) {          // move its first element
  last = slice[end]; slice[end] = slice[0]   // behind the shrinking heap
  siftDown(0, last, end)
}
```

`siftDown` is a `scf.while` that moves an element down until neither
child has to be placed after it.

**2. Stable: binary insertion sort.** O(n log n) comparisons, but O(n^2)
element moves. It is the fallback that always works: a stable sort with
O(n log n) moves needs scratch storage of the operand size (merge sort),
which a dispatch can only take from the stack and which is unbounded for
dynamic sizes.

```
for (i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
  element = slice[i]
  lo = <first position in the sorted prefix [0, i) whose element has to stay
        behind `element`, by binary search>
  for (j = i; j > lo; --j) slice[j] = slice[j - 1]
  slice[lo] = element
}
```

The search uses "strictly before" (comparator true for this order and
false for the opposite one), so that elements the comparator does not
order are never reordered.

**3. Stable with a position operand: heapsort with a tie-break
(canonicalization).** If an operand of a stable sort holds the positions
along the sort dimension (a `linalg.generic` yielding `linalg.index`,
which is what `aten.sort` passes as indices), it tells the input order
of any two elements. `FoldSortStabilityIntoComparator` extends the
comparator to order the elements it does not order itself by position,
and clears `is_stable`:

```mlir
^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_pos: i64, %rhs_pos: i64):
  %before = arith.cmpf oge, %lhs, %rhs : f32
  %after = arith.cmpf oge, %rhs, %lhs : f32
  %ordered = arith.xori %before, %after : i1
  %lower_pos = arith.cmpi slt, %lhs_pos, %rhs_pos : i64
  %result = arith.select %ordered, %before, %lower_pos : i1
  iree_linalg_ext.yield %result : i1
```

The comparator is then a strict total order: no two elements are left
without a defined order, so every sorting algorithm returns the result
of the stable sort and the op can use variant 1. The cost is a second
evaluation of the comparator per comparison.

The rewrite only applies if the sorted positions are used. If they are
not, `RemoveUnusedSortOpResults` drops the operand as before, instead of
keeping its buffer in the dispatch just for the comparator; the sort
then stays stable (variant 2, or variant 4).

**4. Stable but unobservable: heapsort (canonicalization).**
`DropUnobservableSortStability` clears `is_stable` for a single integer
operand whose comparator is an integer comparison of its two arguments.
Elements that such a comparator does not order are the same value, so
their order cannot be observed. Floats are left alone (`0.0` and `-0.0`
compare equal but differ).

### Frontends

* **Torch:** the conversion of `tm_tensor.sort` always sets `is_stable`,
since those sorts have relied on the stable behaviour. With the index
operand of `aten.sort` they get variant 3; a sort that only uses the
values gets variant 2 (floats) or 4 (integers).
* **StableHLO:** `is_stable` of `stablehlo.sort` is passed on. It was
dropped before, and since StableHLO comparators are usually strict,
stable StableHLO sorts were in fact not stable.

### Things to know

* **Unstable sorts order ties differently than before.** That is only
allowed for sorts without `is_stable`, i.e. StableHLO sorts with
`is_stable = false` and ops built directly.
* **NaN.** An ordered float comparison does not order NaN with any
value, which makes the comparator inconsistent (it orders `1.0` and
`2.0`, but neither with NaN). The op description now requires a
consistent comparator. In a simulation of the old lowering on a few
inputs, NaNs stayed at their input positions and the other values were
sorted around them. With the new lowerings the other values can come out
unsorted as well, e.g. `3, NaN, 1, 2, NaN, 5, 4, 0` sorted with `ogt`
gives `NaN, 1, 0, NaN, 5, 4, 2, 3`. A frontend that has to support NaN
keys needs a comparator that orders them (e.g. NaN last, as `torch.sort`
does); the Torch comparators do not do that today.
* `topk_v2` keeps its bubble sort over the k outputs; it is not touched
here.

0.127 ms | 158x |
| 16384 f32, descending | 1 heapsort | 280 ms | 0.515 ms | 544x |
| 512x128 f32, along the inner dimension | 1 heapsort | 1.82 ms | 0.310
ms | 5.9x |
| 128x512 f32, along the outer dimension | 1 heapsort | 9.53 ms | 0.394
ms | 24x |
| stable, 4420 f32 keys + i32 index iota (argsort) | 3 heapsort +

8.2x |

14x |

commit_message:
[LLVMCPU] Move stack allocations over the limit to workgroup local memory

A dispatch whose statically sized temporaries need more than the stack
allocation limit (32 KiB by default) fails to compile with "exceeded stack
allocation limit". An example is `iree_linalg_ext.sort` with a result that is
not used outside the dispatch: its buffer of the full operand size becomes a
`memref.alloca`.

Add a pass that runs before `iree-llvmcpu-assign-workgroup-local-memory`.
When the entry-block allocas of a function exceed the limit, it replaces the
largest ones with `memref.alloc` in the `#iree_codegen.workgroup_local` memory
space until the rest fits, and hands a `memref.memory_space_cast` to the
users. The existing assignment pass lays them out and records the size on the
dispatch config.

Functions within the limit are not changed, so this only affects dispatches
that failed to compile before. Allocations with dynamic sizes stay on the
stack and are still rejected by the check when they exceed the limit.

At run time the dispatch needs that much workgroup local memory. The
local-sync driver allocates it per dispatch. The local-task driver gives each
worker the size of its L2 (or L1) cache unless `--task_worker_local_memory`
is set, and reports RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED when a dispatch needs more.

commit_message:
[LinalgExt] Add is_stable to sort and replace the bubble sort lowering (#25262)

## Context

`iree_linalg_ext.sort` lowers to a bubble sort:
`SortOp::generateScalarImplementation` emits one sweep of n-1
compare-swaps for each of the n iterations of the loop over the sort
dimension, with no early exit. Sorting n elements takes O(n^2) steps,
which shows up as soon as the sorted dimension has a few thousand
elements. We hit this with the argsort of 4420 candidates in the non-max
suppression of a detection model, where the sort dispatch alone took
about 18 ms on x86-64, many times the rest of the model.

A faster in-place algorithm is not stable, and stability turned out to
matter: the bubble sort keeps equal elements in input order when the
comparator is non-strict (`oge`, `sle`, ...), because it then never
swaps them. The Torch frontend emits exactly such comparators, and e.g.
`onnx.NonMaxSuppression` expects the lowest index first among boxes with
the same score (`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes` failed with a
plain heapsort). With a strict comparator (`ogt`, `slt`, ...) the bubble
sort is not stable: keys `1, 1, 2, 2, 0` sorted descending together with
their indices return the indices `3 2 1 0 4`.

So this PR makes stability explicit and picks the algorithm from it.

## This PR

### `is_stable`

The op gets an `is_stable` attribute, false by default and only printed
when set:

```mlir
%0:2 = iree_linalg_ext.sort dimension(0) is_stable(true)
    ins(%keys, %payload : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>)
    outs(%init0, %init1 : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>) {
  ^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_payload: i32, %rhs_payload: i32):
    %before = arith.cmpf ogt, %lhs, %rhs : f32
    iree_linalg_ext.yield %before : i1
} -> tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>
```

The op description now defines the terms. The comparator *does not
order* two elements if it returns the same value for both argument
orders (both `false` with a strict comparison, both `true` with a
non-strict one). Without `is_stable` such elements end up in unspecified
order. With `is_stable` they keep their input order: an element only
moves in front of another one if the comparator returns `true` for that
order and `false` for the opposite one. This definition is the same for
strict and non-strict comparators.

### Lowering variants

All variants are in place: they need no storage besides the operands, so
nothing changes for bufferization or stack usage, and they work for
dynamic sizes and on every backend. The loop nest built from the
iteration domain is unchanged; a slice is sorted in the first iteration
of the loop over the sort dimension, where the inputs were already
copied to the outputs. Operands that are sorted in place are no longer
copied onto themselves.

**1. Not stable: heapsort.** O(n log n) comparisons.

```
for (root = n/2 - 1; root >= 0; --root)      // build the heap
  siftDown(root, slice[root], n)
for (end = n - 1; end > 0; --end) {          // move its first element
  last = slice[end]; slice[end] = slice[0]   // behind the shrinking heap
  siftDown(0, last, end)
}
```

`siftDown` is a `scf.while` that moves an element down until neither
child has to be placed after it.

**2. Stable: binary insertion sort.** O(n log n) comparisons, but O(n^2)
element moves. It is the fallback that always works: a stable sort with
O(n log n) moves needs scratch storage of the operand size (merge sort),
which a dispatch can only take from the stack and which is unbounded for
dynamic sizes.

```
for (i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
  element = slice[i]
  lo = <first position in the sorted prefix [0, i) whose element has to stay
        behind `element`, by binary search>
  for (j = i; j > lo; --j) slice[j] = slice[j - 1]
  slice[lo] = element
}
```

The search uses "strictly before" (comparator true for this order and
false for the opposite one), so that elements the comparator does not
order are never reordered.

**3. Stable with a position operand: heapsort with a tie-break
(canonicalization).** If an operand of a stable sort holds the positions
along the sort dimension (a `linalg.generic` yielding `linalg.index`,
which is what `aten.sort` passes as indices), it tells the input order
of any two elements. `FoldSortStabilityIntoComparator` extends the
comparator to order the elements it does not order itself by position,
and clears `is_stable`:

```mlir
^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_pos: i64, %rhs_pos: i64):
  %before = arith.cmpf oge, %lhs, %rhs : f32
  %after = arith.cmpf oge, %rhs, %lhs : f32
  %ordered = arith.xori %before, %after : i1
  %lower_pos = arith.cmpi slt, %lhs_pos, %rhs_pos : i64
  %result = arith.select %ordered, %before, %lower_pos : i1
  iree_linalg_ext.yield %result : i1
```

The comparator is then a strict total order: no two elements are left
without a defined order, so every sorting algorithm returns the result
of the stable sort and the op can use variant 1. The cost is a second
evaluation of the comparator per comparison.

The rewrite only applies if the sorted positions are used. If they are
not, `RemoveUnusedSortOpResults` drops the operand as before, instead of
keeping its buffer in the dispatch just for the comparator; the sort
then stays stable (variant 2, or variant 4).

**4. Stable but unobservable: heapsort (canonicalization).**
`DropUnobservableSortStability` clears `is_stable` for a single integer
operand whose comparator is an integer comparison of its two arguments.
Elements that such a comparator does not order are the same value, so
their order cannot be observed. Floats are left alone (`0.0` and `-0.0`
compare equal but differ).

### Frontends

* **Torch:** the conversion of `tm_tensor.sort` always sets `is_stable`,
since those sorts have relied on the stable behaviour. With the index
operand of `aten.sort` they get variant 3; a sort that only uses the
values gets variant 2 (floats) or 4 (integers).
* **StableHLO:** `is_stable` of `stablehlo.sort` is passed on. It was
dropped before, and since StableHLO comparators are usually strict,
stable StableHLO sorts were in fact not stable.

### Things to know

* **Unstable sorts order ties differently than before.** That is only
allowed for sorts without `is_stable`, i.e. StableHLO sorts with
`is_stable = false` and ops built directly.
* **NaN.** An ordered float comparison does not order NaN with any
value, which makes the comparator inconsistent (it orders `1.0` and
`2.0`, but neither with NaN). The op description now requires a
consistent comparator. In a simulation of the old lowering on a few

keys needs a comparator that orders them (e.g. NaN last, as `torch.sort`
does); the Torch comparators do not do that today.
* `topk_v2` keeps its bubble sort over the k outputs; it is not touched
here.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 f32, descending | 1 heapsort | 1.08 ms | 0.032 ms | 34x |
| 4420 f32, descending | 1 heapsort | 20.7 ms | 0.125 ms | 166x |
| 4420 f32, already sorted | 1 heapsort | 20.3 ms | 0.113 ms | 180x |
| 4420 f32, reversed | 1 heapsort | 20.3 ms | 0.107 ms | 190x |
| 4420 i32, ascending | 1 heapsort | 10.3 ms | 0.113 ms | 91x |
| 4420 f32 keys + i32 index iota (argsort) | 1 heapsort | 20.1 ms |
0.127 ms | 158x |
| 16384 f32, descending | 1 heapsort | 280 ms | 0.515 ms | 544x |
| 512x128 f32, along the inner dimension | 1 heapsort | 1.82 ms | 0.310
ms | 5.9x |
| 128x512 f32, along the outer dimension | 1 heapsort | 9.53 ms | 0.394

| stable, 4420 f32 keys + i32 index iota (argsort) | 3 heapsort +

| stable, 4420 i32, ascending | 4 heapsort | 10.3 ms | 0.115 ms | 90x |

8.2x |
| stable, 4420 f32, descending | 2 insertion sort | 20.7 ms | 1.48 ms |

commit_message:
[LinalgExt] Add is_stable to sort and replace the bubble sort lowering (#25262)

## Context

`iree_linalg_ext.sort` lowers to a bubble sort:
`SortOp::generateScalarImplementation` emits one sweep of n-1
compare-swaps for each of the n iterations of the loop over the sort
dimension, with no early exit. Sorting n elements takes O(n^2) steps,
which shows up as soon as the sorted dimension has a few thousand
elements. We hit this with the argsort of 4420 candidates in the non-max
suppression of a detection model, where the sort dispatch alone took
about 18 ms on x86-64, many times the rest of the model.

A faster in-place algorithm is not stable, and stability turned out to
matter: the bubble sort keeps equal elements in input order when the
comparator is non-strict (`oge`, `sle`, ...), because it then never
swaps them. The Torch frontend emits exactly such comparators, and e.g.
`onnx.NonMaxSuppression` expects the lowest index first among boxes with
the same score (`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes` failed with a
plain heapsort). With a strict comparator (`ogt`, `slt`, ...) the bubble
sort is not stable: keys `1, 1, 2, 2, 0` sorted descending together with
their indices return the indices `3 2 1 0 4`.

So this PR makes stability explicit and picks the algorithm from it.

## This PR

### `is_stable`

The op gets an `is_stable` attribute, false by default and only printed
when set:

```mlir
%0:2 = iree_linalg_ext.sort dimension(0) is_stable(true)
    ins(%keys, %payload : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>)
    outs(%init0, %init1 : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>) {
  ^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_payload: i32, %rhs_payload: i32):
    %before = arith.cmpf ogt, %lhs, %rhs : f32
    iree_linalg_ext.yield %before : i1
} -> tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>
```

The op description now defines the terms. The comparator *does not
order* two elements if it returns the same value for both argument
orders (both `false` with a strict comparison, both `true` with a
non-strict one). Without `is_stable` such elements end up in unspecified
order. With `is_stable` they keep their input order: an element only
moves in front of another one if the comparator returns `true` for that
order and `false` for the opposite one. This definition is the same for
strict and non-strict comparators.

### Lowering variants

All variants are in place: they need no storage besides the operands, so
nothing changes for bufferization or stack usage, and they work for
dynamic sizes and on every backend. The loop nest built from the
iteration domain is unchanged; a slice is sorted in the first iteration
of the loop over the sort dimension, where the inputs were already
copied to the outputs. Operands that are sorted in place are no longer
copied onto themselves.

**1. Not stable: heapsort.** O(n log n) comparisons.

```
for (root = n/2 - 1; root >= 0; --root)      // build the heap
  siftDown(root, slice[root], n)
for (end = n - 1; end > 0; --end) {          // move its first element
  last = slice[end]; slice[end] = slice[0]   // behind the shrinking heap
  siftDown(0, last, end)
}
```

`siftDown` is a `scf.while` that moves an element down until neither
child has to be placed after it.

**2. Stable: binary insertion sort.** O(n log n) comparisons, but O(n^2)
element moves. It is the fallback that always works: a stable sort with
O(n log n) moves needs scratch storage of the operand size (merge sort),
which a dispatch can only take from the stack and which is unbounded for
dynamic sizes.

```
for (i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
  element = slice[i]
  lo = <first position in the sorted prefix [0, i) whose element has to stay
        behind `element`, by binary search>
  for (j = i; j > lo; --j) slice[j] = slice[j - 1]
  slice[lo] = element
}
```

The search uses "strictly before" (comparator true for this order and
false for the opposite one), so that elements the comparator does not
order are never reordered.

**3. Stable with a position operand: heapsort with a tie-break
(canonicalization).** If an operand of a stable sort holds the positions
along the sort dimension (a `linalg.generic` yielding `linalg.index`,
which is what `aten.sort` passes as indices), it tells the input order
of any two elements. `FoldSortStabilityIntoComparator` extends the
comparator to order the elements it does not order itself by position,
and clears `is_stable`:

```mlir
^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_pos: i64, %rhs_pos: i64):
  %before = arith.cmpf oge, %lhs, %rhs : f32
  %after = arith.cmpf oge, %rhs, %lhs : f32
  %ordered = arith.xori %before, %after : i1
  %lower_pos = arith.cmpi slt, %lhs_pos, %rhs_pos : i64
  %result = arith.select %ordered, %before, %lower_pos : i1
  iree_linalg_ext.yield %result : i1
```

The comparator is then a strict total order: no two elements are left
without a defined order, so every sorting algorithm returns the result
of the stable sort and the op can use variant 1. The cost is a second
evaluation of the comparator per comparison.

The rewrite only applies if the sorted positions are used. If they are
not, `RemoveUnusedSortOpResults` drops the operand as before, instead of
keeping its buffer in the dispatch just for the comparator; the sort
then stays stable (variant 2, or variant 4).

**4. Stable but unobservable: heapsort (canonicalization).**
`DropUnobservableSortStability` clears `is_stable` for a single integer
operand whose comparator is an integer comparison of its two arguments.
Elements that such a comparator does not order are the same value, so
their order cannot be observed. Floats are left alone (`0.0` and `-0.0`
compare equal but differ).

### Frontends

* **Torch:** the conversion of `tm_tensor.sort` always sets `is_stable`,
since those sorts have relied on the stable behaviour. With the index
operand of `aten.sort` they get variant 3; a sort that only uses the
values gets variant 2 (floats) or 4 (integers).
* **StableHLO:** `is_stable` of `stablehlo.sort` is passed on. It was
dropped before, and since StableHLO comparators are usually strict,
stable StableHLO sorts were in fact not stable.

gives `NaN, 1, 0, NaN, 5, 4, 2, 3`. A frontend that has to support NaN
keys needs a comparator that orders them (e.g. NaN last, as `torch.sort`
does); the Torch comparators do not do that today.

here.

commit_message:
[GlobalOptimization] Split constants larger than the max allocation size

A constant whose storage exceeds the max allocation size of its resource
config cannot be packed within that limit. PackConstants places such
constants in a separate resource, but the size will still exceed the limit.
The problem only shows up at runtime, when the device fails to allocate
the buffer.

This adds `iree-global-opt-split-large-constants`. It splits a private,
immutable global above the limit into shards along its outermost non-unit
dimension. Each resulting shard is a contiguous byte range of the original
constant and fits into one allocation. The initial value can be an inline
dense constant, which is sliced, or a named parameter, which is not read: each
shard refers to its byte range of the same parameter through the `offset` and
`length` config entries, relative to any offset the parameter already has. The
uses of its loads are rewritten to use the shards:

* An input of a structured op whose split dimension is indexed by a single
  loop: the op is split along that loop with TilingInterface, one op per
  shard. The results of a parallel loop are inserted into the destination.
  The ops of a reduction loop accumulate into the previous result. This
  covers matmuls with a large weight, such as a tied LM head.
* A value read with `tensor.extract` in the body of an elementwise
  `linalg.generic`, e.g., an embedding lookup: a chain of ops, one per
  shard. Each reads its shard at the rebased, clamped index and keeps the
  previous op's element unless the index lies in its shard.

A constant with any other use is left unchanged with a warning, as is one
that cannot be split: mutable or public globals, values that are neither
inline dense constants nor named parameters, parameters whose length does not
match their type or whose offset is not an integer, element types not stored
at 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits, or a single index of the split dimension that alone
exceeds the limit.

The limit is the max allocation size from `ResourceConfigAttr::lookup`, so
`--iree-stream-resource-max-allocation-size` unless the target sets one. It
defaults to INT64_MAX, so the pass changes nothing unless a limit is set. The
pass runs after transposes have been folded into their consumers, so that an
oversized constant is read by the op that indexes it, and before constant
expressions are hoisted and evaluated into new globals.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Stefan Schuermans <schuermans@roofline.ai>
name: clang-tidy

commit_message:
[DispatchCreation] Count unique tensor operands when limiting fusion (#25256)

I noticed that `wouldExceedOperandLimit` counts defining operations
rather than tensor values. This skips block arguments and counts
distinct results from the same producer once, which can let fusion
exceed the existing operand limit.

This counts unique tensor values instead, while keeping repeated uses
deduplicated.

I've added regressions to the existing `form_dispatch_regions.mlir`
covering block arguments, distinct results from one producer, and
repeated inputs at the limit.

Signed-off-by: anutosh491 <andersonbhat491@gmail.com>
name: setup / setup

commit_message:
[LinalgExt] Add is_stable to sort and lower stable sorts separately

Add an `is_stable` attribute to `iree_linalg_ext.sort`, false by default. A
stable sort keeps elements that the comparator does not order in input order.

* A sort that is not stable lowers to the in-place heapsort.
* A stable sort lowers to an in-place binary insertion sort. It needs no
  storage besides the operands either, so it works for dynamic sizes and on
  all backends, at the cost of O(n^2) element moves.
* Two canonicalizations turn a stable sort into an unstable one when that
  does not change the result: if a used operand holds the positions along
  the sort dimension, the comparator orders the elements it does not order
  itself by position; and a single integer operand compared directly has no
  observable order of equal elements.

The frontends say what they need: the StableHLO conversion passes on
`is_stable`, and the Torch conversion always asks for a stable sort, because
its comparators are non-strict and callers such as `onnx.NonMaxSuppression`
rely on equal elements keeping their order. With the index operand of
`aten.sort` the canonicalization gives these sorts the heapsort. This
replaces the tie-break in the Torch conversion itself.

The lowering is split into documented static functions with explicit
captures instead of nested lambdas, and the op description spells out when a
comparator does not order two elements and that it has to be consistent.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Walbroel <walbroel@roofline.ai>
name: setup / setup

stable sort keeps elements that the comparator does not order in input order.

* A sort that is not stable lowers to the in-place heapsort.
* A stable sort lowers to an in-place binary insertion sort. It needs no
  storage besides the operands either, so it works for dynamic sizes and on
  all backends, at the cost of O(n^2) element moves.
* Two canonicalizations turn a stable sort into an unstable one when that
  does not change the result: if a used operand holds the positions along
  the sort dimension, the comparator orders the elements it does not order
  itself by position; and a single integer operand compared directly has no
  observable order of equal elements.

its comparators are non-strict and callers such as `onnx.NonMaxSuppression`
rely on equal elements keeping their order. With the index operand of
`aten.sort` the canonicalization gives these sorts the heapsort. This
replaces the tie-break in the Torch conversion itself.

captures instead of nested lambdas, and the op description spells out when a
comparator does not order two elements and that it has to be consistent.

commit_message:
[Torch] Order ties of converted sorts by their index operand

The conversion of `aten.sort` emits a non-strict comparator (`oge`, `sle`,
...) and an index operand, and relied on the bubble sort lowering of
`iree_linalg_ext.sort` to keep equal elements in input order: with a
non-strict comparator that lowering never swapped them. The heapsort lowering
does not keep that order, which changes e.g. which of several boxes with the
same score `onnx.NonMaxSuppression` selects first
(`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes`).

When an operand of the converted sort holds the positions along the sort
dimension, extend the comparator: elements that it does not order are ordered
by position. The comparator then is a strict total order and the result is
the one of a stable sort, independent of the algorithm used to sort.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Walbroel <walbroel@roofline.ai>

The conversion of `aten.sort` emits a non-strict comparator (`oge`, `sle`,
...) and an index operand, and relied on the bubble sort lowering of
`iree_linalg_ext.sort` to keep equal elements in input order: with a
non-strict comparator that lowering never swapped them. The heapsort lowering
does not keep that order, which changes e.g. which of several boxes with the
same score `onnx.NonMaxSuppression` selects first
(`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes`).

When an operand of the converted sort holds the positions along the sort
dimension, extend the comparator: elements that it does not order are ordered
by position. The comparator then is a strict total order and the result is
the one of a stable sort, independent of the algorithm used to sort.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Walbroel <walbroel@roofline.ai>

commit_message:
[Torch] Order ties of converted sorts by their index operand

The conversion of `aten.sort` emits a non-strict comparator (`oge`, `sle`,
...) and an index operand, and relied on the bubble sort lowering of
`iree_linalg_ext.sort` to keep equal elements in input order: with a
non-strict comparator that lowering never swapped them. The heapsort lowering
does not keep that order, which changes e.g. which of several boxes with the
same score `onnx.NonMaxSuppression` selects first
(`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes`).

When an operand of the converted sort holds the positions along the sort
dimension, extend the comparator: elements that it does not order are ordered
by position. The comparator then is a strict total order and the result is
the one of a stable sort, independent of the algorithm used to sort.

commit_message:
[Runtime][Python] Preserve DLPack access and ownership (#25227)

Sharing CPU tensors through DLPack must preserve the producer's storage,
access permissions, and lifetime. The fixed import defaults cannot
express host or read-only memory, and unchecked shapes and offsets can
expose invalid memory. Allow callers to specify placement and access,
validate metadata before import, and use the buffer protocol to keep
NumPy views within the mapped range and retain their owner. Make capsule
consumption transfer ownership exactly once, reject exports whose
permissions legacy DLPack cannot represent, and avoid discard mappings
when exporting existing contents.


Assisted-by: Codex

commit_message:
[LLVMCPU] Move stack allocations over the limit to workgroup local memory

A dispatch whose statically sized temporaries need more than the stack
allocation limit (32 KiB by default) fails to compile with "exceeded stack
allocation limit". An example is `iree_linalg_ext.sort` with a result that is
not used outside the dispatch: its buffer of the full operand size becomes a
`memref.alloca`.

Add a pass that runs before `iree-llvmcpu-assign-workgroup-local-memory`.
When the entry-block allocas of a function exceed the limit, it replaces the
largest ones with `memref.alloc` in the `#iree_codegen.workgroup_local` memory
space until the rest fits, and hands a `memref.memory_space_cast` to the
users. The existing assignment pass lays them out and records the size on the
dispatch config.

Functions within the limit are not changed, so this only affects dispatches
that failed to compile before. Allocations with dynamic sizes stay on the
stack and are still rejected by the check when they exceed the limit.

At run time the dispatch needs that much workgroup local memory. The
local-sync driver allocates it per dispatch. The local-task driver gives each
worker the size of its L2 (or L1) cache unless `--task_worker_local_memory`
is set, and reports RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED when a dispatch needs more.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Walbroel <walbroel@roofline.ai>

A dispatch whose statically sized temporaries need more than the stack
allocation limit (32 KiB by default) fails to compile with "exceeded stack
allocation limit". An example is `iree_linalg_ext.sort` with a result that is
not used outside the dispatch: its buffer of the full operand size becomes a
`memref.alloca`.

When the entry-block allocas of a function exceed the limit, it replaces the
largest ones with `memref.alloc` in the `#iree_codegen.workgroup_local` memory
space until the rest fits, and hands a `memref.memory_space_cast` to the
users. The existing assignment pass lays them out and records the size on the
dispatch config.

Functions within the limit are not changed, so this only affects dispatches
that failed to compile before. Allocations with dynamic sizes stay on the
stack and are still rejected by the check when they exceed the limit.

At run time the dispatch needs that much workgroup local memory. The
local-sync driver allocates it per dispatch. The local-task driver gives each
worker the size of its L2 (or L1) cache unless `--task_worker_local_memory`
is set, and reports RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED when a dispatch needs more.

commit_message:
[LLVMCPU] Move stack allocations over the limit to workgroup local memory

A dispatch whose statically sized temporaries need more than the stack
allocation limit (32 KiB by default) fails to compile with "exceeded stack
allocation limit". An example is `iree_linalg_ext.sort` with a result that is
not used outside the dispatch: its buffer of the full operand size becomes a
`memref.alloca`.

Add a pass that runs before `iree-llvmcpu-assign-workgroup-local-memory`.
When the entry-block allocas of a function exceed the limit, it replaces the
largest ones with `memref.alloc` in the `#iree_codegen.workgroup_local` memory
space until the rest fits, and hands a `memref.memory_space_cast` to the
users. The existing assignment pass lays them out and records the size on the
dispatch config.

Functions within the limit are not changed, so this only affects dispatches
that failed to compile before. Allocations with dynamic sizes stay on the
stack and are still rejected by the check when they exceed the limit.

At run time the dispatch needs that much workgroup local memory. The
local-sync driver allocates it per dispatch. The local-task driver gives each
worker the size of its L2 (or L1) cache unless `--task_worker_local_memory`
is set, and reports RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED when a dispatch needs more.

commit_message:
[LinalgExt] Lower sort to an in-place heapsort

`SortOp::generateScalarImplementation` emitted one bubble sort sweep per
iteration of the loop over the sort dimension: n sweeps of n-1 compare-swaps
without early exit, so sorting n elements took O(n^2) steps.

Emit an in-place heapsort instead. It needs O(n log n) comparisons and no
storage besides the operands. The sort of a slice runs in the first iteration
of the loop over the sort dimension, where the inputs were already copied to
the outputs. Operands that are sorted in place are no longer copied onto
themselves.

On an Apple M4 with llvm-cpu, sorting 4420 f32 values takes 0.13 ms instead of
20.7 ms, and 16384 values 0.51 ms instead of 280 ms.

Elements that compare equal can end up in a different order than before. The
previous lowering did not keep their input order for strict comparators
either; the op description now states that the sort is not stable.

commit_message:
[LinalgExt] Lower sort to an in-place heapsort

`SortOp::generateScalarImplementation` emitted one bubble sort sweep per
iteration of the loop over the sort dimension: n sweeps of n-1 compare-swaps
without early exit, so sorting n elements took O(n^2) steps.

Emit an in-place heapsort instead. It needs O(n log n) comparisons and no
storage besides the operands. The sort of a slice runs in the first iteration
of the loop over the sort dimension, where the inputs were already copied to
the outputs. Operands that are sorted in place are no longer copied onto
themselves.

On an Apple M4 with llvm-cpu, sorting 4420 f32 values takes 0.13 ms instead of
20.7 ms, and 16384 values 0.51 ms instead of 280 ms.

Elements that compare equal can end up in a different order than before. The
previous lowering did not keep their input order for strict comparators
either; the op description now states that the sort is not stable.

commit_message:
[GlobalOptimization] change pass ordering so img2col convolutions in quantized conv models will result in integer math (#25099)

Addresses https://github.com/iree-org/iree/issues/25034

Move im2col after the late QDQ conversion and remove the redundant early
QDQ pass, so biased QDQ convolutions convert to integer matmuls after
bias detachment and transpose normalization. Move input demotion
afterward and extend it to generic contractions, preserving f32
accumulation.

Four changes make the single conversion hold up:

- Unit-dim folding shrinks a 1x1 dequantize to rank 0 and leaves an
`expand_shape` between it and the matmul. Reshape fusion by expansion
now handles an empty reassociation for ops without loops, for every op
it supports and in both directions. Only operands that must span every
loop (inits, and the value operand of quantize/dequantize) gain the new
unit dims; scalar parameters stay broadcasts.
- A quantized convolution with a weight zero point needs the sum of
every input window. With QDQ conversion before im2col, that sum
re-gathered every window in its own dispatch and cost about as much as
the im2col itself. The window sum now reads like a ones-filter
convolution, and `ConvertConvToIm2Col` rewrites a convolution without
output-channel reuse when its gather is identical to that of another
rewritten convolution. CSE merges the gathers and the sum becomes a row
reduction over the shared im2col result. Unshared pooling and depthwise
convolutions, dynamic gather shapes and plain matmul sums are
unaffected.
- With im2col after generalization and unit-dim folding, a strided
convolution with a unit window is left with an input access such as `(c,
oh * 2, ow * 2)`, which no longer passes the convolution interface
check. im2col skipped it, and the strided access kept the op from being
data-tiled (the regression reported in review for strided 1x1 shortcut
convolutions). `ConvertConvToIm2Col` now matches on the indexing maps:
an input, a filter and an output, with filter and output maps that are
projected permutations and an input map that is not one but is a sum of
loops scaled by positive constants. Plain contractions, named matmuls
and elementwise ops are left alone; the output-channel reuse and
shared-gather rules are unchanged.
- Unit-dim folding skips named contractions, so the generic that the QDQ
conversion creates from an M = 1 matmul kept its unit loop when
contractions are not generalized. Unit-dim folding now runs on the
function again after the QDQ conversion.

The demotion pass classifies by the contraction and convolution
interfaces and does one rewrite. The multiply-accumulate body check
stays because the convolution interface only inspects indexing maps;
without it a mul+max pooling-like generic would be demoted.

Pipeline regression tests require integer im2col and i8×i8→i32
contractions for biased NHWC/NCHW convolutions, that the window sum
reads the shared gather, and cover generic demotion.

Performance on Apple M4 with llvm-cpu, data tiling and all ukernels,
`--task_topology_performance_level=performance`, median of medians.
NCHW, C_in 16, 28x28 input, C_out 32, activation scale 0.125 and zero
point −1, per-channel weight scale 0.0625 and zero point 2. "Float" is
this branch with `--iree-global-opt-enable-qdq-to-integer-math=false`.

| Case | 1 worker integer | 1 worker float | 4 workers integer | 4
workers float |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 3x3 symmetric | 0.103 ms | 0.117 ms | 0.057 ms | 0.062 ms |
| 3x3 activation zero point only | 0.095 ms | 0.118 ms | 0.052 ms |
0.063 ms |
| 3x3 weight zero point only | 0.063 ms | 0.119 ms | 0.042 ms | 0.070 ms
|
| 3x3 both zero points | 0.065 ms | 0.116 ms | 0.041 ms | 0.063 ms |
| 5x5 both zero points | 0.125 ms | 0.241 ms | 0.060 ms | 0.098 ms |
| 7x7 both zero points | 0.197 ms | 0.369 ms | 0.081 ms | 0.194 ms |
| matmul 676x144x32, both zero points | 0.056 ms | 0.149 ms | 0.045 ms |
0.074 ms |

The gather merges for NCHW and NHWC with stride 2, dilation 2 and batch
2. The integer output is bit-identical to the float path on the tested
inputs; the scales are powers of two, so this does not exercise
rounding.

### Comparison against main

`main` at b4f03e34f7 against this branch, same machine and runtime flags
as above, default task topology restricted to the 4 performance cores,
median of 5 repetitions. All cases use
`--iree-global-opt-use-im2col-for-convs`; "DT" adds
`--iree-opt-data-tiling`, "DT + UK" also adds
`--iree-llvmcpu-enable-ukernels=all`. Shortcut cases are 1x1 QDQ
convolutions with bias and relu, written as channels in → out, input
height, stride.

| QDQ case | No DT: main → PR | DT: main → PR | DT + UK: main → PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| shortcut 256 → 512, 56x56, stride 1 | 14.9 → 14.9 ms | 2.35 → 0.79 ms
| 2.38 → 0.79 ms |
| shortcut 512 → 1024, 28x28, stride 1 | 15.9 → 15.9 ms | 2.15 → 0.66 ms
| 2.15 → 0.66 ms |
| shortcut 1024 → 2048, 14x14, stride 1 | 14.2 → 14.8 ms | 2.11 → 0.55
ms | 2.13 → 0.55 ms |
| shortcut 256 → 512, 56x56, stride 2 | 3.99 → 4.26 ms | 0.67 → 0.22 ms
| 0.68 → 0.22 ms |
| shortcut 512 → 1024, 28x28, stride 2 | 5.70 → 6.01 ms | 0.71 → 0.20 ms
| 0.71 → 0.20 ms |
| shortcut 1024 → 2048, 14x14, stride 2 | 4.01 → 4.35 ms | 0.70 → 0.16
ms | 0.71 → 0.16 ms |
| NHWC 1x1, 512 → 1024, 28x28, stride 2 | 0.71 → 1.23 ms | 0.70 → 0.19
ms | 0.70 → 0.19 ms |
| NCHW 3x3, 64 → 64, 56x56, stride 1, pad 1 | 5.20 → 5.56 ms | 0.92 →
0.52 ms | 0.92 → 0.54 ms |

With data tiling these cases take 0.23x to 0.59x of the time on `main`,
because they now run as `i8 x i8 -> i32` matmuls. Without data tiling
the integer matmul is not faster than the float one: most cases are
within 8%, and the NHWC 1x1 stride 2 case is 1.7x slower.

The run covered 237 case and configuration pairs (quantized and float
convolutions, shortcuts, linear layers, each with and without im2col,
data tiling and ukernels). 192 compile to byte-identical modules on both
sides. The other 45 are the 8 QDQ cases above and 7 float convolutions
with bias, in the three im2col configurations; the float ones are within
noise of `main`. No case loses data tiling. The full ResNet-50 from the
review has not been re-measured.

Compiled with:

```sh
build/tools/iree-compile input.mlir \
  --iree-hal-target-backends=llvm-cpu \
  --iree-llvmcpu-target-cpu=host \
  --iree-global-opt-use-im2col-for-convs \
  --iree-opt-data-tiling \
  --iree-llvmcpu-enable-ukernels=all \
  -o model.vmfb
```

commit_message:
[GlobalOptimization] Split constants larger than the max allocation size

A constant whose storage exceeds the max allocation size of its resource
config cannot be packed within that limit. PackConstants places such
constants in a separate resource, but the size will still exceed the limit.
The problem only shows up at runtime, when the device fails to allocate
the buffer.

This adds `iree-global-opt-split-large-constants`. It splits a private,
immutable global above the limit into shards along its outermost non-unit
dimension. Each resulting shard is a contiguous byte range of the original
constant and fits into one allocation. The initial value can be an inline
dense constant, which is sliced, or a named parameter, which is not read: each
shard refers to its byte range of the same parameter through the `offset` and
`length` config entries, relative to any offset the parameter already has. The
uses of its loads are rewritten to use the shards:

* An input of a structured op whose split dimension is indexed by a single
  loop: the op is split along that loop with TilingInterface, one op per
  shard. The results of a parallel loop are inserted into the destination.
  The ops of a reduction loop accumulate into the previous result. This
  covers matmuls with a large weight, such as a tied LM head.
* A value read with `tensor.extract` in the body of an elementwise
  `linalg.generic`, e.g., an embedding lookup: a chain of ops, one per
  shard. Each reads its shard at the rebased, clamped index and keeps the
  previous op's element unless the index lies in its shard.

A constant with any other use is left unchanged with a warning, as is one
that cannot be split: mutable or public globals, values that are neither
inline dense constants nor named parameters, parameters whose length does not
match their type or whose offset is not an integer, element types not stored
at 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits, or a single index of the split dimension that alone
exceeds the limit.

The limit is the max allocation size from `ResourceConfigAttr::lookup`, so
`--iree-stream-resource-max-allocation-size` unless the target sets one. It
defaults to INT64_MAX, so the pass changes nothing unless a limit is set. The
pass runs after transposes have been folded into their consumers, so that an
oversized constant is read by the op that indexes it, and before constant
expressions are hoisted and evaluated into new globals.
