commit_message:
[LinalgExt] Add is_stable to sort and replace the bubble sort lowering (#25262)

## Context

`iree_linalg_ext.sort` lowers to a bubble sort:
`SortOp::generateScalarImplementation` emits one sweep of n-1
compare-swaps for each of the n iterations of the loop over the sort
dimension, with no early exit. Sorting n elements takes O(n^2) steps,
which shows up as soon as the sorted dimension has a few thousand
elements. We hit this with the argsort of 4420 candidates in the non-max
suppression of a detection model, where the sort dispatch alone took
about 18 ms on x86-64, many times the rest of the model.

A faster in-place algorithm is not stable, and stability turned out to
matter: the bubble sort keeps equal elements in input order when the
comparator is non-strict (`oge`, `sle`, ...), because it then never
swaps them. The Torch frontend emits exactly such comparators, and e.g.
`onnx.NonMaxSuppression` expects the lowest index first among boxes with
the same score (`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes` failed with a
plain heapsort). With a strict comparator (`ogt`, `slt`, ...) the bubble
sort is not stable: keys `1, 1, 2, 2, 0` sorted descending together with
their indices return the indices `3 2 1 0 4`.

So this PR makes stability explicit and picks the algorithm from it.

## This PR

### `is_stable`

The op gets an `is_stable` attribute, false by default and only printed
when set:

```mlir
%0:2 = iree_linalg_ext.sort dimension(0) is_stable(true)
    ins(%keys, %payload : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>)
    outs(%init0, %init1 : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>) {
  ^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_payload: i32, %rhs_payload: i32):
    %before = arith.cmpf ogt, %lhs, %rhs : f32
    iree_linalg_ext.yield %before : i1
} -> tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>
```

The op description now defines the terms. The comparator *does not
order* two elements if it returns the same value for both argument
orders (both `false` with a strict comparison, both `true` with a
non-strict one). Without `is_stable` such elements end up in unspecified
order. With `is_stable` they keep their input order: an element only
moves in front of another one if the comparator returns `true` for that
order and `false` for the opposite one. This definition is the same for
strict and non-strict comparators.

### Lowering variants

All variants are in place: they need no storage besides the operands, so
nothing changes for bufferization or stack usage, and they work for
dynamic sizes and on every backend. The loop nest built from the
iteration domain is unchanged; a slice is sorted in the first iteration
of the loop over the sort dimension, where the inputs were already
copied to the outputs. Operands that are sorted in place are no longer
copied onto themselves.

**1. Not stable: heapsort.** O(n log n) comparisons.

```
for (root = n/2 - 1; root >= 0; --root)      // build the heap
  siftDown(root, slice[root], n)
for (end = n - 1; end > 0; --end) {          // move its first element
  last = slice[end]; slice[end] = slice[0]   // behind the shrinking heap
  siftDown(0, last, end)
}
```

`siftDown` is a `scf.while` that moves an element down until neither
child has to be placed after it.

**2. Stable: binary insertion sort.** O(n log n) comparisons, but O(n^2)
element moves. It is the fallback that always works: a stable sort with
O(n log n) moves needs scratch storage of the operand size (merge sort),
which a dispatch can only take from the stack and which is unbounded for
dynamic sizes.

```
for (i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
  element = slice[i]
  lo = <first position in the sorted prefix [0, i) whose element has to stay
        behind `element`, by binary search>
  for (j = i; j > lo; --j) slice[j] = slice[j - 1]
  slice[lo] = element
}
```

The search uses "strictly before" (comparator true for this order and
false for the opposite one), so that elements the comparator does not
order are never reordered.

**3. Stable with a position operand: heapsort with a tie-break
(canonicalization).** If an operand of a stable sort holds the positions
along the sort dimension (a `linalg.generic` yielding `linalg.index`,
which is what `aten.sort` passes as indices), it tells the input order
of any two elements. `FoldSortStabilityIntoComparator` extends the
comparator to order the elements it does not order itself by position,
and clears `is_stable`:

```mlir
^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_pos: i64, %rhs_pos: i64):
  %before = arith.cmpf oge, %lhs, %rhs : f32
  %after = arith.cmpf oge, %rhs, %lhs : f32
  %ordered = arith.xori %before, %after : i1
  %lower_pos = arith.cmpi slt, %lhs_pos, %rhs_pos : i64
  %result = arith.select %ordered, %before, %lower_pos : i1
  iree_linalg_ext.yield %result : i1
```

The comparator is then a strict total order: no two elements are left
without a defined order, so every sorting algorithm returns the result
of the stable sort and the op can use variant 1. The cost is a second
evaluation of the comparator per comparison.

The rewrite only applies if the sorted positions are used. If they are
not, `RemoveUnusedSortOpResults` drops the operand as before, instead of
keeping its buffer in the dispatch just for the comparator; the sort
then stays stable (variant 2, or variant 4).

**4. Stable but unobservable: heapsort (canonicalization).**
`DropUnobservableSortStability` clears `is_stable` for a single integer
operand whose comparator is an integer comparison of its two arguments.
Elements that such a comparator does not order are the same value, so
their order cannot be observed. Floats are left alone (`0.0` and `-0.0`
compare equal but differ).

### Frontends

* **Torch:** the conversion of `tm_tensor.sort` always sets `is_stable`,
since those sorts have relied on the stable behaviour. With the index
operand of `aten.sort` they get variant 3; a sort that only uses the
values gets variant 2 (floats) or 4 (integers).
* **StableHLO:** `is_stable` of `stablehlo.sort` is passed on. It was
dropped before, and since StableHLO comparators are usually strict,
stable StableHLO sorts were in fact not stable.

### Things to know

* **Unstable sorts order ties differently than before.** That is only
allowed for sorts without `is_stable`, i.e. StableHLO sorts with
`is_stable = false` and ops built directly.
* **NaN.** An ordered float comparison does not order NaN with any
value, which makes the comparator inconsistent (it orders `1.0` and
`2.0`, but neither with NaN). The op description now requires a
consistent comparator. In a simulation of the old lowering on a few
inputs, NaNs stayed at their input positions and the other values were
sorted around them. With the new lowerings the other values can come out
unsorted as well, e.g. `3, NaN, 1, 2, NaN, 5, 4, 0` sorted with `ogt`
gives `NaN, 1, 0, NaN, 5, 4, 2, 3`. A frontend that has to support NaN
keys needs a comparator that orders them (e.g. NaN last, as `torch.sort`
does); the Torch comparators do not do that today.
* `topk_v2` keeps its bubble sort over the k outputs; it is not touched
here.

## Performance

Apple M4, llvm-cpu, `local-task`, median of 5 repetitions. Each program
generates pseudo-random keys and sorts them with a single
`iree_linalg_ext.sort`; the times include generating the keys (about
0.01 ms for 4420 elements). The `main` column is the same program
without `is_stable`, which `main` does not have.

| program | variant | main | this PR | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 f32, descending | 1 heapsort | 1.08 ms | 0.032 ms | 34x |
| 4420 f32, descending | 1 heapsort | 20.7 ms | 0.125 ms | 166x |
| 4420 f32, already sorted | 1 heapsort | 20.3 ms | 0.113 ms | 180x |
| 4420 f32, reversed | 1 heapsort | 20.3 ms | 0.107 ms | 190x |
| 4420 i32, ascending | 1 heapsort | 10.3 ms | 0.113 ms | 91x |
| 4420 f32 keys + i32 index iota (argsort) | 1 heapsort | 20.1 ms |
0.127 ms | 158x |
| 16384 f32, descending | 1 heapsort | 280 ms | 0.515 ms | 544x |
| 512x128 f32, along the inner dimension | 1 heapsort | 1.82 ms | 0.310
ms | 5.9x |
| 128x512 f32, along the outer dimension | 1 heapsort | 9.53 ms | 0.394
ms | 24x |
| stable, 4420 f32 keys + i32 index iota (argsort) | 3 heapsort +
tie-break | 20.1 ms | 0.236 ms | 85x |
| stable, 4420 i32, ascending | 4 heapsort | 10.3 ms | 0.115 ms | 90x |
| stable, 1024 f32, descending | 2 insertion sort | 1.08 ms | 0.131 ms |
8.2x |
| stable, 4420 f32, descending | 2 insertion sort | 20.7 ms | 1.48 ms |
14x |
| stable, 4420 f32, already sorted | 2 insertion sort | 20.3 ms | 0.067
ms | 303x |
| stable, 4420 f32, reversed | 2 insertion sort | 20.3 ms | 2.69 ms |
7.6x |
| stable, 4420 f32 keys + i32 payload | 2 insertion sort | 20.1 ms |
1.79 ms | 11x |
| stable, 16384 f32, descending | 2 insertion sort | 280 ms | 17.9 ms |
16x |

The tie-break of variant 3 costs a bit less than 2x over the plain
heapsort. The element-move loop of the insertion sort is not vectorized
by LLVM at the moment (about one element per cycle); if stable sorts
without a position operand turn out to matter, that loop is where to
look.

## Tests

* `LinalgExt/IR/test/roundtrip.mlir`: the attribute.
* `LinalgExt/IR/test/canonicalize.mlir`: variant 3 applies with used
positions along the sort dimension, and not for positions along another
dimension, unused positions, or a sort that is not stable; variant 4
applies to a plain integer comparison, and not to floats or a comparator
that does more than compare its arguments.
* `LinalgExt/Transforms/test/convert_to_loops.mlir`: the heapsort and
the insertion sort structure; `sort_multi` has one operand that is not
sorted in place, to cover the copy.
* Torch and StableHLO conversion tests: `is_stable` is set / passed on.
* `tests/e2e/linalg_ext_ops/sort.mlir`: eight more tests: odd length
with duplicate and negative keys, a single element, the inner dimension,
keys with indices, a tie-break comparator on many equal keys, and stable
sorts of many equal keys with a strict comparator, a non-strict one, and
a position operand.
* Run locally: the e2e file passes on llvm-cpu, VMVX and Metal, and
compiles for Vulkan SPIR-V. `test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes`
from iree-test-suites passes at O0 and O2. I could not run CUDA/ROCm or
the full Torch and ONNX suites locally.

commit_message:
[LinalgExt] Add is_stable to sort and replace the bubble sort lowering (#25262)

## Context

`iree_linalg_ext.sort` lowers to a bubble sort:
`SortOp::generateScalarImplementation` emits one sweep of n-1
compare-swaps for each of the n iterations of the loop over the sort
dimension, with no early exit. Sorting n elements takes O(n^2) steps,
which shows up as soon as the sorted dimension has a few thousand
elements. We hit this with the argsort of 4420 candidates in the non-max
suppression of a detection model, where the sort dispatch alone took
about 18 ms on x86-64, many times the rest of the model.

A faster in-place algorithm is not stable, and stability turned out to
matter: the bubble sort keeps equal elements in input order when the
comparator is non-strict (`oge`, `sle`, ...), because it then never
swaps them. The Torch frontend emits exactly such comparators, and e.g.
`onnx.NonMaxSuppression` expects the lowest index first among boxes with
the same score (`test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes` failed with a
plain heapsort). With a strict comparator (`ogt`, `slt`, ...) the bubble
sort is not stable: keys `1, 1, 2, 2, 0` sorted descending together with
their indices return the indices `3 2 1 0 4`.

So this PR makes stability explicit and picks the algorithm from it.

## This PR

### `is_stable`

The op gets an `is_stable` attribute, false by default and only printed
when set:

```mlir
%0:2 = iree_linalg_ext.sort dimension(0) is_stable(true)
    ins(%keys, %payload : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>)
    outs(%init0, %init1 : tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>) {
  ^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_payload: i32, %rhs_payload: i32):
    %before = arith.cmpf ogt, %lhs, %rhs : f32
    iree_linalg_ext.yield %before : i1
} -> tensor<?xf32>, tensor<?xi32>
```

The op description now defines the terms. The comparator *does not
order* two elements if it returns the same value for both argument
orders (both `false` with a strict comparison, both `true` with a
non-strict one). Without `is_stable` such elements end up in unspecified
order. With `is_stable` they keep their input order: an element only
moves in front of another one if the comparator returns `true` for that
order and `false` for the opposite one. This definition is the same for
strict and non-strict comparators.

### Lowering variants

All variants are in place: they need no storage besides the operands, so
nothing changes for bufferization or stack usage, and they work for
dynamic sizes and on every backend. The loop nest built from the
iteration domain is unchanged; a slice is sorted in the first iteration
of the loop over the sort dimension, where the inputs were already
copied to the outputs. Operands that are sorted in place are no longer
copied onto themselves.

**1. Not stable: heapsort.** O(n log n) comparisons.

```
for (root = n/2 - 1; root >= 0; --root)      // build the heap
  siftDown(root, slice[root], n)
for (end = n - 1; end > 0; --end) {          // move its first element
  last = slice[end]; slice[end] = slice[0]   // behind the shrinking heap
  siftDown(0, last, end)
}
```

`siftDown` is a `scf.while` that moves an element down until neither
child has to be placed after it.

**2. Stable: binary insertion sort.** O(n log n) comparisons, but O(n^2)
element moves. It is the fallback that always works: a stable sort with
O(n log n) moves needs scratch storage of the operand size (merge sort),
which a dispatch can only take from the stack and which is unbounded for
dynamic sizes.

```
for (i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
  element = slice[i]
  lo = <first position in the sorted prefix [0, i) whose element has to stay
        behind `element`, by binary search>
  for (j = i; j > lo; --j) slice[j] = slice[j - 1]
  slice[lo] = element
}
```

The search uses "strictly before" (comparator true for this order and
false for the opposite one), so that elements the comparator does not
order are never reordered.

**3. Stable with a position operand: heapsort with a tie-break
(canonicalization).** If an operand of a stable sort holds the positions
along the sort dimension (a `linalg.generic` yielding `linalg.index`,
which is what `aten.sort` passes as indices), it tells the input order
of any two elements. `FoldSortStabilityIntoComparator` extends the
comparator to order the elements it does not order itself by position,
and clears `is_stable`:

```mlir
^bb0(%lhs: f32, %rhs: f32, %lhs_pos: i64, %rhs_pos: i64):
  %before = arith.cmpf oge, %lhs, %rhs : f32
  %after = arith.cmpf oge, %rhs, %lhs : f32
  %ordered = arith.xori %before, %after : i1
  %lower_pos = arith.cmpi slt, %lhs_pos, %rhs_pos : i64
  %result = arith.select %ordered, %before, %lower_pos : i1
  iree_linalg_ext.yield %result : i1
```

The comparator is then a strict total order: no two elements are left
without a defined order, so every sorting algorithm returns the result
of the stable sort and the op can use variant 1. The cost is a second
evaluation of the comparator per comparison.

The rewrite only applies if the sorted positions are used. If they are
not, `RemoveUnusedSortOpResults` drops the operand as before, instead of
keeping its buffer in the dispatch just for the comparator; the sort
then stays stable (variant 2, or variant 4).

**4. Stable but unobservable: heapsort (canonicalization).**
`DropUnobservableSortStability` clears `is_stable` for a single integer
operand whose comparator is an integer comparison of its two arguments.
Elements that such a comparator does not order are the same value, so
their order cannot be observed. Floats are left alone (`0.0` and `-0.0`
compare equal but differ).

### Frontends

* **Torch:** the conversion of `tm_tensor.sort` always sets `is_stable`,
since those sorts have relied on the stable behaviour. With the index
operand of `aten.sort` they get variant 3; a sort that only uses the
values gets variant 2 (floats) or 4 (integers).
* **StableHLO:** `is_stable` of `stablehlo.sort` is passed on. It was
dropped before, and since StableHLO comparators are usually strict,
stable StableHLO sorts were in fact not stable.

### Things to know

* **Unstable sorts order ties differently than before.** That is only
allowed for sorts without `is_stable`, i.e. StableHLO sorts with
`is_stable = false` and ops built directly.
* **NaN.** An ordered float comparison does not order NaN with any
value, which makes the comparator inconsistent (it orders `1.0` and
`2.0`, but neither with NaN). The op description now requires a
consistent comparator. In a simulation of the old lowering on a few
inputs, NaNs stayed at their input positions and the other values were
sorted around them. With the new lowerings the other values can come out
unsorted as well, e.g. `3, NaN, 1, 2, NaN, 5, 4, 0` sorted with `ogt`
gives `NaN, 1, 0, NaN, 5, 4, 2, 3`. A frontend that has to support NaN
keys needs a comparator that orders them (e.g. NaN last, as `torch.sort`
does); the Torch comparators do not do that today.
* `topk_v2` keeps its bubble sort over the k outputs; it is not touched
here.

## Performance

Apple M4, llvm-cpu, `local-task`, median of 5 repetitions. Each program
generates pseudo-random keys and sorts them with a single
`iree_linalg_ext.sort`; the times include generating the keys (about
0.01 ms for 4420 elements). The `main` column is the same program
without `is_stable`, which `main` does not have.

| program | variant | main | this PR | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 f32, descending | 1 heapsort | 1.08 ms | 0.032 ms | 34x |
| 4420 f32, descending | 1 heapsort | 20.7 ms | 0.125 ms | 166x |
| 4420 f32, already sorted | 1 heapsort | 20.3 ms | 0.113 ms | 180x |
| 4420 f32, reversed | 1 heapsort | 20.3 ms | 0.107 ms | 190x |
| 4420 i32, ascending | 1 heapsort | 10.3 ms | 0.113 ms | 91x |
| 4420 f32 keys + i32 index iota (argsort) | 1 heapsort | 20.1 ms |
0.127 ms | 158x |
| 16384 f32, descending | 1 heapsort | 280 ms | 0.515 ms | 544x |
| 512x128 f32, along the inner dimension | 1 heapsort | 1.82 ms | 0.310
ms | 5.9x |
| 128x512 f32, along the outer dimension | 1 heapsort | 9.53 ms | 0.394
ms | 24x |
| stable, 4420 f32 keys + i32 index iota (argsort) | 3 heapsort +
tie-break | 20.1 ms | 0.236 ms | 85x |
| stable, 4420 i32, ascending | 4 heapsort | 10.3 ms | 0.115 ms | 90x |
| stable, 1024 f32, descending | 2 insertion sort | 1.08 ms | 0.131 ms |
8.2x |
| stable, 4420 f32, descending | 2 insertion sort | 20.7 ms | 1.48 ms |
14x |
| stable, 4420 f32, already sorted | 2 insertion sort | 20.3 ms | 0.067
ms | 303x |
| stable, 4420 f32, reversed | 2 insertion sort | 20.3 ms | 2.69 ms |
7.6x |
| stable, 4420 f32 keys + i32 payload | 2 insertion sort | 20.1 ms |
1.79 ms | 11x |
| stable, 16384 f32, descending | 2 insertion sort | 280 ms | 17.9 ms |
16x |

The tie-break of variant 3 costs a bit less than 2x over the plain
heapsort. The element-move loop of the insertion sort is not vectorized
by LLVM at the moment (about one element per cycle); if stable sorts
without a position operand turn out to matter, that loop is where to
look.

## Tests

* `LinalgExt/IR/test/roundtrip.mlir`: the attribute.
* `LinalgExt/IR/test/canonicalize.mlir`: variant 3 applies with used
positions along the sort dimension, and not for positions along another
dimension, unused positions, or a sort that is not stable; variant 4
applies to a plain integer comparison, and not to floats or a comparator
that does more than compare its arguments.
* `LinalgExt/Transforms/test/convert_to_loops.mlir`: the heapsort and
the insertion sort structure; `sort_multi` has one operand that is not
sorted in place, to cover the copy.
* Torch and StableHLO conversion tests: `is_stable` is set / passed on.
* `tests/e2e/linalg_ext_ops/sort.mlir`: eight more tests: odd length
with duplicate and negative keys, a single element, the inner dimension,
keys with indices, a tie-break comparator on many equal keys, and stable
sorts of many equal keys with a strict comparator, a non-strict one, and
a position operand.
* Run locally: the e2e file passes on llvm-cpu, VMVX and Metal, and
compiles for Vulkan SPIR-V. `test_nonmaxsuppression_identical_boxes`
from iree-test-suites passes at O0 and O2. I could not run CUDA/ROCm or
the full Torch and ONNX suites locally.

commit_message:
[Codegen] Make the padding loops of foldPadIntoMapStore disjoint

foldPadIntoMapStore writes the padding value with one loop nest for the
low and one for the high padding of each dimension. Each loop nest spans
the full range of all other dimensions, so the nests overlap where the
padding of two dimensions intersects. The nests are distributed to
workgroups independently, so two workgroups can write the same element
concurrently. Both write the same value, so the results are correct,
but it is a data race.

Since #24534, i8 matmuls on the inner_tiled data-tiling path for x86
with AVX-512 VNNI use the 16x16x2 intrinsic, and the relayout of its
swizzled accumulator becomes a map_store with padding in both
dimensions. ThreadSanitizer reports the overlapping writes in
e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_inner_tiled_i8_i32 and
e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_inner_tiled_llvm_ukernel_i8_i32, so
linux_x64_clang_tsan fails whenever it runs on a host with AVX-512
VNNI. Other hosts skip these tests.

The loop nests of a dimension now only span the unpadded range of the
dimensions before it. Every padding element is then written exactly
once, by the loop nest of the first dimension in which it lies in the
padding. Apart from the narrower bounds, the loop nests and their
distribution are unchanged, so the overlapping stores are simply
dropped. This affects both the CPU and the GPU combine-layout passes.

Tested with a ThreadSanitizer build of the runtime on a host with
AVX-512 VNNI: both tests report 12 races without this change and none
with it.

performance numbers. The other dtypes are being tracked here: #24932

tile.

commit_message:
[CI] Fail the Clang Tidy job on clang-tidy findings

Make clang-tidy findings on changed lines fail the job, so that new code
has to be clang-tidy clean. False positives can be suppressed with
`// NOLINT(<check-name>)`.

With the generated headers available, clang-tidy 19 and the current
compiler configuration report 32 findings on the lines changed in the
last 200 commits. Of the last 50 workflow runs that ran clang-tidy, one
reported a finding, the false positive above.

The job also has to be a required status check to block merging.

commit_message:
[CI] Enable more clang-tidy checks for the runtime

The runtime configuration only runs the clang diagnostics and the static
analyzer. Enable checks for bug-prone patterns, uninitialized variables,
nested conditional operators and functions that are not thread-safe,
plus readability checks that apply to C:

- bugprone-* and misc-*, with the exclusions of the compiler
  configuration. Also excluded, because they flag common C idioms or the
  runtime's structure:
  - bugprone-multi-level-implicit-pointer-conversion: `T **` passed as
    `const void *`, e.g. to memcpy.
  - bugprone-switch-missing-default-case: the bytecode dispatch
    switches.
  - misc-header-include-cycle: the iree/base/api.h umbrella header.
- cppcoreguidelines-init-variables: local variables without an
  initializer.
- readability-avoid-nested-conditional-operator, and the readability
  checks for duplicate includes, redundant declarations, control flow
  and preprocessor directives, misleading indentation, misplaced array
  indices, inconsistent parameter names, boolean expressions and
  unconditional `#if`s.
- concurrency-mt-unsafe: functions that are not thread-safe, since the
  runtime is multi-threaded.
- cert-env33-c, cert-err34-c and cert-flp30-c: calls to system(),
  string-to-number conversions without error checking and floating-point
  loop counters.

As for the compiler configuration in #23203, the configuration was run
with clang-tidy 19 on the runtime lines changed in the last 200 commits.
The current configuration reports nothing there. The new one reports 6
findings:

- a uint16_t loop counter compared with an iree_host_size_t size in the
  bytecode verifier, which never terminates for sizes above 65535,
- a macro in the bytecode verifier that declares `__i`, a reserved
  identifier,
- three status variables without an initializer,
- one nested conditional operator in a test.

Left out because they were noisy on those commits or do not match the
runtime's style: readability-braces-around-statements (40 warnings),
readability-isolate-declaration (6), readability-else-after-return (3)
and cert-err33-c (3, unused fprintf results).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Tobias Fuchs <fuchs@roofline.ai>
name: Test ONNX / test_onnx_models :: amdgpu_hip_rdna4

commit_message:
[Stream] Respect the parameter offset in SplitParameterEncoder

A named parameter can refer to a byte range of an archive entry. The
`offset` and `length` entries of its config give that range. The encoder
used the length, as the parameter's storage size, but always loaded from
offset 0. So it read the wrong bytes for any parameter with a nonzero
offset.

The encoder now loads from the parameter's offset. A parameter without an
offset still loads from 0.

The new test loads 1024 bytes at offset 4096. It checks both the copy of
the unmodified parameter and the input of a hoisted fill.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Stefan Schuermans <schuermans@roofline.ai>
name: linux_x64_bazel / linux_x64_bazel

A named parameter can refer to a byte range of an archive entry. The
`offset` and `length` entries of its config give that range. The encoder
used the length, as the parameter's storage size, but always loaded from
offset 0. So it read the wrong bytes for any parameter with a nonzero
offset.

The encoder now loads from the parameter's offset. A parameter without an
offset still loads from 0.

The new test loads 1024 bytes at offset 4096. It checks both the copy of
the unmodified parameter and the input of a hoisted fill.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Stefan Schuermans <schuermans@roofline.ai>
name: Test ONNX / test_onnx_models :: amdgpu_hip_rdna4
